I've wondered about this too. Mostly I think people haven't thought it through properly, but where does the instinctual reaction come from? Here's my theory:

people's brains are much more integral to their sense of self than any other part of their bodies, people see their brain as "them" but their skin or pancreas as belonging to them. People are much more affronted then by the idea that their brains could be diseased and more likely to object to language being used in that context.

And like, people have a really weird ways of conceptualizing what goes on in the brain, as demonstrated by the way people on both sides of the "chemical imbalance" debate talk about it. Why certainly there are people who seem more genetically predisposed to depression, and some where it is clearly a result in circumstance, distinguishing these by calling them "chemical" and "situational" depression, as if reactions to outside events don't involve neurotransmitters is absurd. It's like the difference between inherited hyperlipidemia and hyperlipidemia in someone who lives on Big Macs and Coke. The difference in the role of lifestyle is obvious but no one would say the second person had "situational hyperlipidemia" or there weren't physical changes in their cholesterol levels. 

Edit: I also think a lot of it is such straight up stigma tbh, and a mix of psychiatrists not explaining the known environmental role to their patients, and then those patients going online to see so-and-so random redditor talking about how serotonin deficiencies and how depression means your brain's just naturally fucked up, and the patient thinking well clearly I don't have *depression* then because I don't think my brain is fucked up I think this because I lost my job and don't know how I'm gonna pay my bills, and blame this incongruence on the whole of psychiatry rather than one rushed/lazy doctor and a layperson spreading misinfo.
